```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

Kim 2023 fitted ten candidate release functions to in vivo release data of the
levonorgestrel (LNG) 150 mg two-rod subdermal implant (Jadelle) and carried two
of them forward as the input function of a whole-body PBPK model. Both are
packaged here as release-only models:

* `Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_firstOrderRelease`:
  `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_firstOrderRelease"))$description`
* `Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_biexpRelease`:
  `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_biexpRelease"))$description`
* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_firstOrderRelease"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics15051393>
* Supplement (Table S1, Figure S1): <https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/pharmaceutics15051393/s1>

The PBPK model the release functions feed (built in PK-Sim / MoBi, from Cicali
2021, doi:10.1002/psp4.12572) is a platform model whose organ volumes, flows
and partition coefficients are not printed in either paper, so it is not part
of this package. The packaged models carry the release step only; their
outputs are the cumulative amount released from the implant (`released`, mg)
and the instantaneous release rate (`releaseRate`, mg/day).

# Population

The release functions were fitted to group-mean data, not to individual
subjects (Section 2.2 and Figure 2):

* LNG content of explanted implants by time since insertion, from Callahan 2015
  and Fuchs 2020 (two-rod implants removed for analysis up to 5 years after
  insertion; content measured by spectroscopy with HPLC confirmation). Released
  amount is the loaded 150 mg minus the measured residual content.
* The in vivo release rates of the Jadelle US product label -- about
  0.1 mg/day at month 1, 0.04 mg/day at 12 months and 0.03 mg/day from 24
  months -- converted to a released amount.

All subjects were healthy women using the implant for contraception. The paper
does not state how many explants contributed. The n = 321 in its abstract is
the Jadelle clinical-trial PK cohort used to check the PBPK model (Figure 3),
not the release fit. The same information is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_firstOrderRelease")()$population`.

# Source trace

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| First-order release, `Q(t) = Qmax * (1 - exp(-k1 * t))` | n/a | Table 1, Weibull row, special case l = 1; Equation (1) |
| Biexponential release, `Q(t) = Dose - Qb1 * exp(-kb1 * t) - (Dose - Qb1) * exp(-kb2 * t)` | n/a | Table 1, Biexponential row |
| Implant load `Dose` (both models) | 150 mg (fixed) | Table 2 |
| `lfdepot` (first-order; `Qmax / Dose`) | log(67.86 / 150) | Table 2 (Qmax = 67.86 mg); Section 3.1 ("45.3% of original LNG load") |
| `lka` (first-order; `k1`) | log(0.0009) /day | Table 2 |
| `logitfrel` (biexponential; `Qb1 / Dose`) | logit(44.64 / 150) | Table 2 (Qb1 = 44.64 mg) |
| `lka_fast` (biexponential; `k1b`) | log(0.00127) /day | Table 2 |
| `lka_slow` (biexponential; `k2b`) | log(8.985e-5) /day | Table 2 |
| Residual error, inter-individual variability | none | Section 2.2 (unweighted nonlinear least squares; no variance reported) |

Table 2 and Supplementary Table S1 print identical values for both models.

# Simulation

Each model is dosed with the 150 mg implant load at insertion (time 0). The
biexponential model takes the load twice -- once into `depot`, once into
`depot2` -- and splits it between the two pools by bioavailability, so the two
records together release the full 150 mg once.

```{r models}
mod_fo <- rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb("Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_firstOrderRelease"))
mod_be <- rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb("Kim_2023_levonorgestrel_biexpRelease"))

days_per_month <- 365.25 / 12
obs_days <- seq(0, 60, by = 0.5) * days_per_month
load_mg <- 150

implant_events <- function(dose_cmts) {
  doses <- data.frame(id = 1L, time = 0, amt = load_mg, cmt = dose_cmts, evid = 1L)
  obs <- data.frame(id = 1L, time = obs_days, amt = 0, cmt = "released", evid = 0L)
  dplyr::bind_rows(doses, obs)
}

solve_release <- function(mod, dose_cmts, label) {
  sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = implant_events(dose_cmts),
                         rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12)
  as.data.frame(sim) |>
    dplyr::transmute(model = label, time, months = time / days_per_month,
                     released, releaseRate)
}

sim <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  solve_release(mod_fo, "depot", "First-order"),
  solve_release(mod_be, c("depot", "depot2"), "Biexponential")
)
```

## Check against the published closed forms

The ODE solutions must reproduce the Table 1 release functions evaluated at
the Table 2 estimates. Both sides use the same parameters, so the only
difference is integration error.

```{r closed-form}
closed_form <- function(model, t) {
  ifelse(
    model == "First-order",
    67.86 * (1 - exp(-0.0009 * t)),
    load_mg - 44.64 * exp(-0.00127 * t) - (load_mg - 44.64) * exp(-8.985e-5 * t)
  )
}
closed_rate <- function(model, t) {
  ifelse(
    model == "First-order",
    67.86 * 0.0009 * exp(-0.0009 * t),
    0.00127 * 44.64 * exp(-0.00127 * t) +
      8.985e-5 * (load_mg - 44.64) * exp(-8.985e-5 * t)
  )
}
chk <- sim |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    err_q = abs(released - closed_form(model, time)),
    err_rate = abs(releaseRate - closed_rate(model, time))
  )
chk |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(max_abs_err_mg = max(err_q), max_abs_err_mg_per_day = max(err_rate))
# Measured integration error is about 3e-11 mg at rtol = 1e-10; a transcription
# error in any parameter moves the 5-year released amount by whole milligrams.
stopifnot(max(chk$err_q) < 1e-5, max(chk$err_rate) < 1e-8)
```

## Replicate Figure 2 (First-order and Biexponential panels)

```{r fig2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
label_rates <- data.frame(months = c(1, 12, 24), releaseRate = c(0.1, 0.04, 0.03))

sim_long <- sim |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(released, releaseRate), names_to = "output", values_to = "value") |>
  dplyr::mutate(output = dplyr::recode(output,
    released = "LNG released (mg)",
    releaseRate = "LNG release rate (mg/day)"
  ))
label_long <- label_rates |>
  dplyr::rename(value = releaseRate) |>
  dplyr::mutate(output = "LNG release rate (mg/day)")

ggplot(sim_long, aes(months, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = tidyr::crossing(label_long, model = unique(sim$model)),
             colour = "blue", size = 2) +
  facet_grid(output ~ model, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 60, by = 12)) +
  labs(x = "Months of use", y = NULL,
       caption = "Replicates the First-order and Biexponential panels of Figure 2 of Kim 2023 (typical curves; points: Jadelle label release rates).") +
  theme_bw()
```

Both models start near 0.06 mg/day and fall to 0.03 mg/day by 24 months,
matching the label's 12- and 24-month rates; neither reaches the label's
0.1 mg/day at month 1, as in the paper's Figure 2. By 60 months both have
released about 55-56 mg, the level of the last explant data point in Figure 2.

## Published release landmarks

```{r landmarks}
at_month <- function(m) sim |> dplyr::filter(abs(months - m) < 1e-8)
landmarks <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  at_month(1) |> dplyr::mutate(quantity = "Release rate at 1 month (mg/day)",
                               simulated = releaseRate, published = 0.1),
  at_month(12) |> dplyr::mutate(quantity = "Release rate at 12 months (mg/day)",
                                simulated = releaseRate, published = 0.04),
  at_month(24) |> dplyr::mutate(quantity = "Release rate at 24 months (mg/day)",
                                simulated = releaseRate, published = 0.03)
) |>
  dplyr::transmute(model, quantity, simulated = signif(simulated, 3), published,
                   pct_diff = round(100 * (simulated / published - 1), 1))
landmarks |>
  dplyr::rename(Model = model, Quantity = quantity, Simulated = simulated,
                `Jadelle label` = published, `% difference` = pct_diff) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The 12- and 24-month rates are 4-12% above the label. The month-1 rate is
36-41% below the label for both models; the paper's Figure 2 shows the same
shortfall, since neither function reproduces the initial burst.

```{r landmark-check}
later <- dplyr::filter(landmarks, !grepl("1 month", quantity))
stopifnot(all(abs(later$pct_diff) < 15))
```

The first-order releasable fraction is `fdepot = 67.86 / 150 =`
`r round(100 * 67.86 / 150, 1)`% of the load, the paper's "45.3% of original
LNG load", close to the 50% non-releasable fraction the authors assumed from ex
vivo data at the end of a five-year trial (Section 2.3).

# Sino-implant (II) fits

To check the robustness of the approach, Kim 2023 refitted both functions to
the Sino-implant (II) explant data of Callahan 2015 and reported the estimates
in the text of Section 3.1 (to fewer significant digits than Table 2): Qmax
75.6 mg and k1 0.0008 /day for the first-order model; Qb1 14.95 mg, k1b
0.0062 /day and k2b 0.0002 /day for the biexponential model. They are not
packaged as separate models, but they can be applied to the packaged models
through `ini()`:

```{r sino}
mod_fo_sino <- mod_fo |> rxode2::ini(lfdepot = log(75.6 / 150), lka = log(0.0008))
mod_be_sino <- mod_be |>
  rxode2::ini(logitfrel = log((14.95 / 150) / (1 - 14.95 / 150)),
              lka_fast = log(0.0062), lka_slow = log(0.0002))

sim_sino <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  solve_release(mod_fo_sino, "depot", "First-order"),
  solve_release(mod_be_sino, c("depot", "depot2"), "Biexponential")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(implant = "Sino-implant (II)")

dplyr::bind_rows(dplyr::mutate(sim, implant = "Jadelle"), sim_sino) |>
  ggplot(aes(months, released, colour = implant)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 60, by = 12)) +
  labs(x = "Months of use", y = "LNG released (mg)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Jadelle (Table 2) versus Sino-implant (II) (Section 3.1) estimates.") +
  theme_bw()
```

The paper interprets the Sino-implant biexponential fit as about 9.97% of the
load released over roughly 5 months (1/0.0062 days) and the remaining 90.03%
released slowly. The packaged parameterisation reproduces that split:

```{r sino-split}
sino_theta <- mod_be_sino$theta
sino_split <- c(
  fast_pool_pct = 100 * rxode2::expit(sino_theta[["logitfrel"]]),
  fast_pool_mean_days = 1 / exp(sino_theta[["lka_fast"]])
)
sino_split
# The paper's own figures: 9.97% of the load, over about 5 months (161 days).
stopifnot(abs(sino_split[["fast_pool_pct"]] - 9.97) < 0.01,
          abs(sino_split[["fast_pool_mean_days"]] - 161.3) < 0.1)
```

# PKNCA

Not applicable. The packaged models describe release from the implant only and
produce no concentration, so there is nothing for noncompartmental analysis to
summarise. The release checks above (closed-form identity and the published
release-rate landmarks) are the validation. To predict plasma levonorgestrel,
couple `releaseRate` to a levonorgestrel disposition model -- for example by
replacing the `released` sink with that model's `central` compartment.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Release-only.** The paper's systemic predictions (Figure 3) come from a
  PK-Sim / MoBi whole-body PBPK model whose structure is not printed, so they
  cannot be reproduced here and are not checked.
* **No residual error or variability.** The functions were fitted by
  unweighted nonlinear least squares to mean data (Section 2.2). Neither a
  residual variance nor any inter-individual variability was reported, so the
  models are deterministic. The 95% prediction bands of Figure 2 are not
  reproducible from the printed results.
* **Fractions instead of amounts.** The paper estimates `Qmax` and `Qb1` in mg
  with the load fixed at 150 mg. They are stored as the fractions
  `fdepot = Qmax / 150` and `frel = Qb1 / 150` so the models are dose-driven.
  For a 150 mg implant the result is identical to the published functions
  (checked above). Using a different load assumes the releasable and fast-pool
  fractions scale with the load, which the paper did not test.
* **Equation (1) versus Table 2.** The PBPK input function of Equation (1) is
  written with a non-releasable fraction `f` "assumed to be 50%" (Section 2.3),
  while the fitted `Qmax = 67.86 mg` implies `f = 0.548`; the paper notes that
  `Qmax` is derived from `(1 - f) * Dose`. The packaged model uses the fitted
  Table 2 value.
* **Equation (2) versus Table 1.** Equation (2), the biexponential PBPK input,
  multiplies the whole biexponential by `(1 - f)`, but the fitted function in
  Table 1 releases the full 150 mg (no `f`). Applying `(1 - f) = 0.5` would
  halve every release rate and contradict the release-rate panel of Figure 2,
  so the packaged model follows Tables 1 and 2.
* **Wide confidence intervals.** All three biexponential estimates have 95%
  confidence intervals that span zero (Table 2); the paper chose the model for
  its biphasic mechanism rather than its precision (Section 4).
* **Candidate models not packaged.** Eight further release functions (Weibull,
  second-order, Korsmeyer-Peppas, Higuchi, zero-order, Hixson-Crowell,
  Peppas-Sahlin, Population Council) were fitted in the model-selection step
  and their estimates are in Supplementary Table S1. The paper did not carry
  them forward -- the polynomial forms have no upper bound on the released
  amount, and the second-order fit has a negative adjusted R-squared -- so they
  are not packaged.
* **Month conversion.** Figure axes in months are converted with
  365.25 / 12 days per month.
* **Errata.** A EuropePMC search (2026-10-26) found no correction notice for
  this article.
